case_info.scenario: A woman in her early 50s presented with a neck mass, incidentally discovered during evaluation of recurrent headaches. She reported mild solid food dysphagia but was otherwise asymptomatic. Physical examination revealed fullness in the location of the left thyroid lobe. Flexible laryngoscopy showed normal vocal fold movement and laboratory findings were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed a 2.4-cm hypoechoic nodule posterior to the left thyroid lobe, with suggestion of a feeding vessel (Figure 1). An ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration for the presumed thyroid nodule was performed, but definitive characterization was not possible with the limited material obtained. Therefore, a 20-gauge core biopsy was attempted but was aborted due to patient discomfort. Because of the unclear diagnosis, she was scheduled for a left thyroid lobectomy with excision of the mass. Postoperatively, she experienced resolution of her dysphagia and vocal fold function was normal.
case_info.caption: Hypoechoic nodule posterior to left thyroid lobe in the axial plane and in the sagittal planes.
case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

dialogue_history.text: Given the presentation of the hypoechoic nodule and the necessity for surgical intervention due to diagnostic uncertainty, the most appropriate next step in management is to prepare for a definitive pathological analysis post-thyroid lobectomy. Based on the characteristics of the nodule, the suspicion leans towards papillary thyroid carcinoma (B), which is common in this demographic and can present as a hypoechoic lesion. The resolution of her dysphagia and normal vocal fold function postoperatively further supports that the mass was likely compressive. Therefore, I would prioritize further pathological assessment of the excised tissue.

user_state.reasoning: The characteristics of the nodule and the patient's demographics raise suspicion for thyroid carcinoma, particularly papillary carcinoma.

dialogue_history.speaker: medical
dialogue_history.text: I agree that definitive pathology from the excised specimen is crucial, but given the nodule's location posterior to the thyroid lobe and the suggestive feeding vessel on ultrasound, we should also consider a parathyroid lesion, such as a parathyroid adenoma, which can cause compressive symptoms. The incomplete preoperative cytology and aborted core biopsy make surgical exploration and excision the correct diagnostic and therapeutic step. The pathology will confirm whether it's a thyroid neoplasm or an extrathyroidal entity.

metadata.belief: The excised mass is most likely a parathyroid adenoma, given its posterior extrathyroidal location, suggestion of a feeding vessel on ultrasound, and presentation with dysphagia that resolved postoperatively.
metadata.reasoning: The ultrasound and clinical features are atypical for a primary thyroid nodule and more suggestive of a parathyroid lesion.

dialogue_history.text: While I acknowledge the possibility of a parathyroid adenoma due to the nodule's location and feeding vessel, the clinical context and the characteristics of the hypoechoic nodule strongly suggest papillary thyroid carcinoma. The demographics and typical presentation align more closely with thyroid malignancy, making my priority the pathological evaluation of the excised tissue. We can reassess based on the pathology results postoperatively, but my current stance remains that papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most likely diagnosis.

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically

  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still

* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]

[Role]

Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal.

Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 2.2. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.

     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.       not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is

  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

She reported mild solid food dysphagia but was otherwise asymptomatic. Physical examination revealed fullness in the location of the left thyroid lobe. case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5
